title: Aim for a Plentiful Harvest — Full Teaching
text:
There comes a point in the life of every believer when Christianity can no longer remain something we merely believe.
It must become something that happens to us.
Something that enters the heart, cleans the heart, orders the mind, disciplines the body, redirects our gifts, changes the way we treat people—and finally produces something that did not exist before.
Because God did not plant a garden in you merely so that the soil could remain empty.
Aim for a plentiful harvest.
And I believe there are seven things we must understand.
First: do not negotiate with sin.
Sin is like weed. Sin rarely enters the heart announcing that it intends to destroy you.
It begins small.
A thought.
A desire.
A resentment.
A fantasy.
A little bitterness.
A little envy.
A little compromise that says, I have a right to remain here.
And that is the dangerous moment.
Because a weed is easiest to remove when it is still a weed.
Leave it alone long enough and it develops roots.
Leave the roots long enough and you no longer have one weed—you have a field.
And leave the field long enough and the good seed begins fighting simply to survive.
So when sin appears, do not entertain it.
Do not interview it.
Do not build a house for it and then ask God to remove the tenant.
Pull it out.
Pray immediately.
Reject it immediately.
Turn your mind immediately.
If you fall, rise immediately.
The great mistake is not merely falling.
The great mistake is allowing what made you fall to become comfortable inside you.
Your heart belongs to God.
Sin has no right of residence there.


Second: fight sin as something Christ has already defeated.
There are Christians who fight sin as though Jesus has not yet risen.
Every failure becomes despair.
Every fall becomes an identity.
Every weakness becomes evidence that God has abandoned them.
No.
There is a difference between taking sin seriously and believing sin is stronger than Christ.
The Christian does not say:
“I have never fallen.”
The Christian says:
“I will not make my fall my home.”
Christ has already opened the door back.
He has already provided cleansing.
He has already paid the debt.
So repentance is not crawling toward a God who is searching for an excuse to destroy you.
It is the child coming home to the Father who has already made reconciliation possible.
Fight consistently.
But fight with hope.
Repent seriously.
But repent with confidence.
Do not glorify your sin by behaving as though it has more power to condemn than Christ has power to save.
The blood of Christ is greater than the stain of sin.


Third: stop trying to live Christianity without the Holy Spirit.
Many people are trying to operate a spiritual life using nothing but personal effort and human intelligence.
They wake up.
Plan and plan again
Run around.
Make decisions.
Get confused.
Get angry when things don’t go their way.
And pray never pausing to listen to what God may have to say to them.
But the Holy Spirit was not given merely to decorate Christianity.
The Holy Spirit was given to lead us into communion with God.
To teach.
To correct.
To remind.
To strengthen.
To reveal.
To direct.
It is the power of waking up and asking:
“Lord, what are You doing today, and where do You want me inside it?”
Imagine prayer becoming more than a ritual.
It is bringing your work to God.
Your marriage.
Your business.
Your fears.
Your gifts.
Your confusion.
Your decisions.
Imagine asking Him to water what you have planted.
To uproot what should never have grown.
To show you where to go.
To tell you when to stop.
To tell you when to move.
That is communion.
And communion should become so natural that prayer is not something we occasionally perform.
It becomes the atmosphere in which we live.


Fourth: discipline is how gifts become fruit.
Everybody admires gifts.
Very few people respect discipline until they discover that gifts without discipline eventually rot.
You may be intelligent.
You may be persuasive.
You may be beautiful.
You may be creative.
You may be wealthy.
You may have an extraordinary ability to influence people.
But the question is not merely:
What were you given?
The question is:
What did you multiply?
One servant received five talents.
Another received two.
Another received one.
God did not judge them because their starting points were unequal.
He judged what they did with what they received.
That means you must stop comparing your field with another man's field.
Work your own land.
If God gave you thirty seeds, produce sixty.
If He gave you sixty, aim for a hundred.
Discipline is not punishment.
Discipline is the structure that allows potential to become service.
You wake when you should wake.
You pray when you should pray.
You work when you should work.
You restrain yourself when restraint is necessary.
You continue after excitement disappears.
Because discipline is not about becoming rigid.
Discipline is about becoming fruitful.


Fifth: humility is not thinking less of yourself.
Humility is refusing to lie about yourself.
That is all.
Look carefully at the things people boast about.
Where they were born.
Who their father was.
What family they came from.
Their intelligence.
Their beauty.
Their nationality.
Their social class.
Their talents.
How many of those things did they personally manufacture?
You did not select your DNA.
You did not choose the brain you were born with.
You did not command the world to place you in the family where you arrived.
That is providence.
And humility is simply refusing to steal credit for providence.
But humility goes even deeper.
Even the gifts you genuinely developed still require breath.
Health.
Opportunity.
Time.
Teachers.
Circumstances.
Grace.
So humility is not saying:
“I am worthless.”
Humility says:
“Whatever is truly good in me should return to the One from whom goodness came.”
And then humility becomes service.
If God gave you influence—use it.
If He gave you intelligence—use it.
If He gave you money—use it.
If He gave you strength—use it.
Not merely to enlarge your name.
But to enlarge the amount of good that passes through your life.
Look at Christ.
When people wanted to glorify Him, He continually pointed toward the Father.
When people were healed, He could say:
“Your faith has healed you.”
Think about that.
All that prayer.
All that obedience.
All that holiness.
All that sacrifice.
And still no desperation to advertise Himself.
And what happened?
The One who refused to seize glory for Himself had heaven speak on His behalf.
There is a lesson there.
If you stop spending your life trying to announce yourself, perhaps you will leave room for God to announce what matters.


Sixth: Be a man after God’s heart. Learn the system of God.
The world has one accounting system.
God appears to have another.
The world says:
Give where you will receive something back.
Christ says:
Give where they cannot repay you—and God will repay you.
The world says:
Make sure everybody knows what you did.
Christ says:
Give secretly—and your Father who sees in secret remembers.
The world says:
Money is valuable because you can keep it.
Christ says:
Use temporary wealth to create treasure that survives you.
The world says:
Serve important people.
Christ says:
What you did for the least, you did for Me.
The world says:
Retaliate.
Protect your pride.
Make them pay.
Christ says:
Forgive—and enter the jurisdiction of mercy.
The world says:
Hate your enemy.
Christ says:
Love your enemy.
This is God's will.
Give something that doesn't last to people who cannot repay you —
money,
time,
food,
forgiveness,
attention,
comfort,
a visit,
a cup of water—
and God will give you something that lasts.
You give forgiveness.
God sees it.
You endure humiliation.
God sees it.
You give to somebody who does not know your name.
God sees it.
You quietly rescue a sinner.
God sees it.
You help somebody bear more fruit.
God sees it.
This is why faith matters.
Because to the world sometimes, righteousness looks like loss and foolishness.
But if you trust God, you will reap bountifully. If you do not trust God, you will seek immediate payments.
Immediate revenge.
Immediate applause.
Immediate pleasure.
Immediate recognition.
Immediate return.
No. Faith says:
“My debt is a seed to be repaid by a just and perfect God.”


Seventh: bear fruit.
Because everything comes here eventually.
Why remove the weeds?
So something else can grow.
Why overcome sin?
So you can be free to love.
Why seek the Holy Spirit and the kingdom?
So God can dwell in you.
Why become disciplined?
So your gifts can multiply.
Why become humble?
So the fruit tells about the vinedresser.
Why forgive?
So bitterness does not consume the field.
Why give?
So that you circulate what God gave.
The climax of spiritual maturity is not that you stopped doing bad things.
It’s rather a sign of spiritual fertility.
A barren field can contain few weeds.
It is still barren.
The purpose of clearing the land is fruit.
Christ did not only say:
I did not commit adultery.
I did not steal.
I did not murder.
He spoke about something more demanding.
I was hungry—did you feed Me?
I was lonely—were you there?
I was sick—did you come?
That is fruit.
And fruit requires labor.
Everybody loves beginnings.
Beginning the marriage.
Beginning the mission.
Beginning the business.
Beginning is exciting.
But fruit does not grow because you started.
Fruit grows because you continued.
The next day.
And the next day.
You continued when the field looked empty.
You continued when nobody applauded.
Until one day the invisible became visible.
That is spiritual maturity.
Not avoiding hell.
Not calling yourself saved.
Not surviving temptation.
But becoming the kind of person through whom goodness reaches others.
So pull the weeds.
Remember the victory.
Walk with the Spirit.
Discipline yourself.
Be humble.
Trust the justice and mercy of God.
And then—
bear fruit.
Thirtyfold.
Sixtyfold.
A hundredfold.
Plant something good in the garden each day.
